subject: Estimating abundance across species distribution using pcount() estimates

messages.author: 021ce6f755780301
messages.subject: Estimating abundance across species distribution using pcount() estimates
parts:
Hi,

I'm currently researching various methods for modeling my data (see
below), and it seems like the N-mixture model with a ZIP distribution
for abundance (using 'unmarked' pcount() function) is the most
appropriate, given the source of zeros; however, before I dive in,
there is one issue I'm stuck on:

My data set consists of A) counts of shorebirds during winter (3 to 6
counts per winter, maximum 1 per month) at >150 coastal sites and B)
shoreline units for our entire study region, each characterized by
substrate type, exposure, and other environmental attributes. The goal
of our project is to 1) model the relationship between the abundance
of shorebirds and shoreline characteristics, and 2) to estimate the
total abundance of each shorebird species within the entire study
region based on these relationships.

I've been reading through the relevant literature and noticed in both
a thread in this forum and in a paper by Joseph et al. (2009) that
"the abundance estimates produced by N-mixture models are estimates of
the number of species that UTILIZE a site, rather than the true
density". This is particularly true if the birds are not always
available to be detected - which I believe to be true for shorebirds.

Is there a way to use the N-mixture model to estimate total abundance
across the species' distribution then? From what I understand, it
sounds like the predict() function will overestimate abundance in this
case.

Please let me know if anything is unclear - while I'm not new to R or
mixed-effects models, I am somewhat new to N-Mixture with zero-
inflation, and particularly using these models for prediction.

Thanks!

Cheers,
Jenn

messages.author: 527e14923215b7e4
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Estimating abundance across species distribution using pcount() estimates
parts:
Hi Jenn,

The N-mixture model requires that the local populations are closed during the study period.  Is that likely to be true for your 6 month study? If not, you might look through some of the references on the help pages for gmultmix() and pcountOpen().

Richard

messages.author: 021ce6f755780301
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Estimating abundance across species distribution using pcount() estimates
parts:
Hi Richard,

Thanks for the reply - and to Steffan as well who replied with more or less then same comment.

I have definitely questioned whether our study meets the population closure assumption as well: One of the primary species we're studying are Pacific Dunlin, and I believe the population can more or less be considered closed, as several studies have shown that the birds settle into their wintering sites in October and remain more or less in the same area until spring migration. That said, I have some concerns that even local movements would violate the assumption, as the scale of the analysis (i.e., sites) is a likely smaller (more fine) then the scale of "local" movements. It's also true that sudden changes in weather (e.g., a mudflat freezing over) could force the birds to another area. While the situation is definitely different than if we were studying migrants, I'm still not sure if closure is a realistic assumption. I'm not the shorebird expert; however, given that our end goal is to predict total population size, inflating this value by under-estimating detection probability (i.e., due to an open population) is definitely something we'd want to avoid.

So that leads me to pcountOpen(): The same initial question I asked still applies in this case, as well as any suggestions on how one goes about parametrizing gamma and omega (??? I wouldn't even know what values to being with here!).

Thanks.

Cheers,
Jenn

messages.author: 527e14923215b7e4
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Estimating abundance across species distribution using pcount() estimates
parts:
Hi Jenn,

If the population is open to movement and/or mortality, it may be hard to get a good estimate of population size without "robust design" type data. It would be worthwhile to read the papers describing the models fit by pcountOpen() and gmultmix(), and to consult some texts like Williams et al. (2002).

Richard
